result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.dfs_postorder_nodes()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} List nodes in depth-first postorder. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L48467-L48555){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.dfs_postorder_nodes( source=None, depth_limit=None, mode="out", ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![DFS postorder](/assets/graphs/dfs-postorder-nodes.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A seven-node tree searched depth-first from the root A (outlined). Numbered badges give the order nodes finish: D and E finish before their parent B, F and G before C, and the root A finishes last. The card lists D, E, B, F, G, C, A, beside the preorder A, B, D, E, C, F, G that dfs() returns." width="100%"} In a depth-first search, a node is *finished* once every node below it has been explored. Postorder lists nodes in the order they finish, so every node comes after all of its DFS descendants. This is the order to process a tree bottom-up (children before parents), and in a DAG, the reverse of the postorder is a topological order. `dfs()` gives the complementary preorder, the order nodes are first reached. With `source=None` (default), the search covers every node, restarting from unvisited nodes in ID order. Neighbors are explored in edge insertion order, as in `dfs()`. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [source]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str, None]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : The starting node, as an integer ID or a string label. If `None` (default), search from every unvisited node in turn. [depth_limit]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Do not go deeper than this many hops from the start of each tree. Nodes at the limit are still listed (NetworkX's `dfs_postorder_nodes()` omits them, unlike its preorder). If `None` (default), there is no limit. [mode]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [["out"]{.st}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Which way to follow edges on a directed graph: `"out"` (default), `"in"`, or `"all"`. Ignored for undirected graphs. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Node IDs in postorder. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the node does not exist, `depth_limit=` is negative, or `mode=` is invalid. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} In a small tree, the leaves finish first and the root last: ::: {#52d11580 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec tree = ( ec.Graph(directed=True) .add_nodes(["root", "a", "b", "a1", "a2"]) .add_edges([("root", "a"), ("root", "b"), ("a", "a1"), ("a", "a2")]) ) [tree.get_label_from_id(n) for n in tree.dfs_postorder_nodes("root")] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` ['a1', 'a2', 'a', 'b', 'root'] ``` ::: ::: Reversing the postorder of a DAG gives a valid topological order: ::: {#f94afd80 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} order = list(reversed(tree.dfs_postorder_nodes())) position = {n: i for i, n in enumerate(order)} all(position[s] < position[t] for _, s, t in tree.get_edges_as_tuples()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` True ``` ::: :::
